name: Amazon Route 53
summary: AWS’s authoritative DNS and domain registrar, with health checks and routing by latency, location or weight.
intro: Route 53 hosts your domain’s records in a hosted zone: public zones answer the internet, and private zones answer only inside the VPCs you attach them to. Each record has a routing policy that decides which answer a query gets. Simple returns one value. Weighted splits traffic by percentage, which is handy for canary releases. Latency sends users to the AWS Region that answers them fastest. Failover switches to a standby when a health check fails. Geolocation, geoproximity, IP-based and multivalue answer cover the rest.

Its AWS-specific feature is the alias record. A normal CNAME can’t sit at the bare domain (`example.com`), but an alias can, and it points straight at a CloudFront distribution, a load balancer, an API Gateway domain or an S3 website. Route 53 follows that resource’s IP addresses as they change, and queries to alias records for AWS resources are free. A hosted zone costs $0.50 a month for the first 25, and standard queries $0.40 per million.
strengths: Alias records work at the zone apex and cost nothing to query when they point at AWS resources
Health checks plus failover, latency and weighted routing give you DNS-level traffic steering
Private hosted zones give VPCs internal names without running your own DNS servers
Registrar, DNS and certificate validation all in one AWS account
limits: DNS failover is only as fast as resolvers honour TTLs; clients may keep a stale answer for a while
Latency and geolocation queries cost more than standard ones ($0.60 and $0.70 per million)
Alias records only point at a set list of AWS resources; anything else needs a CNAME
Health checks are billed per check per month: $0.50 for AWS endpoints (the first 50 in your account are free) and $0.75 for others

story: By 2010 you could run almost a whole application on AWS, but not its name. DNS still lived with a registrar, a specialist DNS company or your own BIND servers, configured separately from the EC2 instances and load balancers it pointed at, whose addresses changed as you scaled. Getting DNS wrong takes a site offline as surely as losing its servers.

AWS announced Amazon Route 53 on 5 December 2010 and made it generally available in May 2011, adding weighted routing and integration with Elastic Load Balancing. The “53” is the TCP and UDP port DNS servers listen on. Its name servers sit on a global anycast network, so each query is answered by a nearby location. In 2012 latency-based routing brought “the same latency based routing technology that powers Amazon CloudFront” to customers’ own records.
Route 53 then took on more of the job: health checks and DNS failover in 2013, domain registration and private zones for VPCs in 2014, and resolvers for hybrid networks in 2018.

choices.choice: Anycast name servers around the world
choices.why: Many locations announce the same addresses, so resolvers reach the closest one and traffic shifts to another site automatically if one fails.

DNS hosts are frequent DDoS targets. Route 53 gives each domain its own set of four out of 2,048 virtual name servers, so an attack on one domain is unlikely to take out every server another domain depends on.

Load balancer IP addresses change, and a CNAME isn’t allowed at a bare domain. An alias looks up the resource’s current addresses itself, so `example.com` can point straight at a load balancer or CloudFront.
Customers wanted apps that span several Regions. Weighted, latency and failover policies let the DNS answer itself steer users, with no extra proxy in the path.

timeline.text: Generally available in May with weighted routing and load balancer aliases
Domain registration, geolocation routing and private hosted zones for VPCs
Route 53 Resolver links VPC and on-premises DNS
Global Resolver, an internet-reachable anycast DNS resolver for an organization’s own clients, becomes generally available
